messages.content: I want to design a tiered MVCC storage engine that preserves snapshot isolation and reclaims old versions safely, even when migration, writes, and crashes overlap. How should I frame the goal?

The goal has two parts that must hold together. First, the engine must preserve snapshot isolation while versions move between tiers and while versions are reclaimed. An acknowledged write, or a version still required by a snapshot, must survive a crash at every migration and reclamation transition. Second, migration must increase p99 read latency by no more than 20% compared with an identical workload run without migration. Neither correctness nor the latency bound is optional.
When you say snapshot isolation, what is the important point for this design?

A snapshot read must continue to see the versions appropriate to its snapshot, rather than having its view change merely because storage is migrating or reclaiming versions. The design therefore has to distinguish a version that is old but still snapshot-required from one that is no longer needed. Tier placement should not determine whether a snapshot can see a version.
So moving a version and removing a version are different questions?

Yes. Migration concerns where a version resides; reclamation concerns whether it can be discarded. A move must not make an acknowledged write or a snapshot-required version disappear across a crash. Reclamation is safe only when discarding a version cannot remove one that a snapshot still requires. That distinction matters particularly when a write and a migration are concurrent: the design must account for whichever version the snapshot is entitled to read, without assuming that activity has paused.
Does the crash requirement apply only once a migration finishes?

No. It explicitly applies at every migration and reclamation transition. It is not enough for the final placement to be durable if a crash during an intermediate transition could lose an acknowledged write or a snapshot-required version. The same concern applies while reclamation is in progress, not just after a version has been removed.
Would it be accurate to describe that as a requirement on every crash point, rather than on steady states alone?

Yes. The design needs to be sound if a crash interrupts a transition, as well as when the engine is in a stable state. At each such point, acknowledged writes and snapshot-required versions must still survive. That statement sets the required outcome; it does not, by itself, prescribe a particular migration protocol or recovery mechanism.
What does the word ‘acknowledged’ add to the write requirement?

It identifies the writes for which the engine has already reported success. The design cannot treat an acknowledged write as expendable because a migration is underway or reclamation is being considered. The stated requirement is specifically that acknowledged writes survive crashes at every migration and reclamation transition; it does not specify a durability mechanism or change the meaning of an acknowledgment.
And why mention snapshot-required versions separately if writes are already covered?

Because preserving acknowledged writes alone does not express the full MVCC obligation. A snapshot may still require a particular historical version to produce its view. The design must preserve that version across those crash points even if newer writes exist. Conversely, the goal does not say to retain every historical version forever: it singles out versions that are still snapshot-required.
How should I think about concurrent migration and writes without assuming an implementation?

Treat concurrency as part of the correctness condition, not as a special case that can be ignored. If a write occurs while migration is changing placement, the resulting state must still preserve the acknowledged write across a crash. Reads must still obtain versions consistent with their snapshots, and reclamation must not remove versions those snapshots require. Those are observable obligations; the goal leaves open how the engine coordinates the activities.
Could I satisfy snapshot isolation during ordinary operation but still fail this goal?

Yes. A design could return appropriate versions while it is running yet fail to preserve an acknowledged write or a snapshot-required version if a crash occurs partway through migration or reclamation. This goal requires both correct snapshot behavior during concurrent activity and survival at every specified transition. Checking only uninterrupted operation would leave out the crash condition.
What about a version that is old but might be used by a snapshot?

Its age alone is not enough to justify reclamation. The relevant question is whether a snapshot still requires it. If it does, the version must remain available for that snapshot and survive crashes at migration and reclamation transitions. The goal does not provide a particular rule for determining when that need ends, so that rule should not be assumed here.
Does ‘tiered’ tell us which tier must hold a required version?

No specific tier placement is stated. The engine is tiered, and migration is part of the setting, but the requirement is about preserving the required versions and writes, not assigning them to a named tier. A snapshot’s correct view must not depend on a required version remaining in its former location.
I also want to keep the performance target precise. How do I state the 20% limit?

For an identical workload, compare p99 read latency with migration against p99 read latency without migration. The former may be at most 1.20 times the latter. This is a relative limit on p99 read latency, not an allowance of 20 milliseconds, 20 percentile points, or an unspecified average-latency increase.
Why is the ‘identical workloads’ phrase important?

It defines the comparison. The p99 read-latency increase is attributed to migration only if the migration and no-migration cases use identical workloads. Otherwise, a workload difference could change the p99 independently of migration. The goal gives that comparison but does not specify a particular workload, a measurement procedure, or a measured result.
Does meeting the read-latency limit relax any of the crash requirements?

No. Migration increasing p99 read latency by at most 20% versus an identical workload without migration is one requirement; survival of acknowledged writes and snapshot-required versions at every migration and reclamation transition is another. A fast migration that loses a required version after a crash would not meet the goal. Nor would crash-safe migration automatically satisfy the p99 constraint.
Could I phrase the safety condition as ‘don’t reclaim until the migration is done’?

That would be narrower than the stated goal and would not, on its own, establish safety. Reclamation must be safe in the presence of concurrent migration, writes, and crashes. Whether a particular version may be reclaimed depends on whether it is still snapshot-required and whether the required crash-survival property remains intact. The goal does not prescribe a blanket scheduling rule.
What should a review of the design ask at a migration or reclamation boundary?

At each boundary, it should ask whether every acknowledged write still survives a crash, whether every snapshot-required version still survives a crash, and whether snapshot reads retain the view they are entitled to despite concurrent activity. Separately, it should ask whether migration’s p99 read latency remains within 20% of the no-migration p99 for an identical workload. These questions express the criteria without assuming a specific implementation or claiming they have already been met.
So the design target is not simply ‘move versions safely’; it is to preserve the right versions through every overlap and keep the read tail under the stated limit?

Exactly. The target is a tiered MVCC storage engine that preserves snapshot isolation and safe reclamation during concurrent migration, writes, and crashes. Acknowledged writes and snapshot-required versions must survive crashes at every migration and reclamation transition, while migration increases p99 read latency by at most 20% versus identical workloads without migration.

For that tiered MVCC engine, I propose fsync-before-ack MVCC WAL, durable snapshot pins, copy-fsync-then-publish manifests, pin-gated reclamation, and read-priority migration throttling. Can you explain how those pieces fit together?

They divide the goal into related responsibilities. The fsync-before-ack MVCC write-ahead log (WAL) addresses acknowledged writes. Durable snapshot pins represent versions that must remain available to snapshots across crashes. Copy-fsync-then-publish manifests govern when a migrated copy becomes visible as a placement change. Pin-gated reclamation prevents removal while a snapshot still requires a version. Read-priority migration throttling addresses migration’s effect on read latency. Together, they are a proposed approach, not yet a demonstrated guarantee that every crash point or the p99 limit is satisfied.
Start with the WAL. What does ‘fsync-before-ack’ commit us to?

It means the relevant MVCC WAL record is fsynced before the engine acknowledges the write. The ordering matters: an acknowledgment should not precede the durability step on which that acknowledged write relies. In this proposal, the WAL supplies a durable record of MVCC writes while their placement in the tiers may be changing. That explains the WAL’s role, without assuming a specific log format or recovery procedure.
Why call out MVCC in the WAL description?

Because the engine must preserve versions, not merely the latest value. Referring to an MVCC WAL makes clear that the durability proposal is meant to support versioned writes and snapshot isolation. It does not specify exactly what fields a record contains or how versions are reconstructed; those details would need their own design.
Would fsync-before-ack alone protect a long-running snapshot?

No. It addresses when a write can be acknowledged, but it does not by itself say which older version a snapshot still needs or prevent that version from being reclaimed. Durable snapshot pins and pin-gated reclamation cover that separate obligation. The distinction is important because a version can remain necessary to a snapshot even after newer writes have been acknowledged.
What is a durable snapshot pin meant to express?

It is a durable indication that a snapshot has a continuing need for the versions in its view. ‘Durable’ matters because a crash during migration or reclamation must not erase the protection for a version that is still snapshot-required. The proposal names the protection mechanism, but it does not prescribe a pin representation or the exact way pins are created and released.
How does pin-gated reclamation use that indication?

Reclamation is gated by the pins: it must not discard a version while a pin indicates that a snapshot still requires it. That makes reclaimability a separate question from whether a version is old or whether it has been copied to another tier. Because the pins are durable, the proposed gate is meant to continue protecting snapshot-required versions across a crash, not only during uninterrupted operation.
Does a pin imply that every old version is retained?

No. The proposal uses pins to distinguish versions that remain snapshot-required from versions that may become eligible for reclamation. It does not require indefinite retention of all historical versions. Equally, the absence of a stated pin format is not a license to infer a particular eligibility rule; the key proposal here is that reclamation is gated by durable snapshot needs.
Now unpack ‘copy-fsync-then-publish manifests.’ What order is it proposing?

First make the migrated copy, then fsync that copy, and only then publish the manifest change that makes the new placement visible. The ordering is the point: publication should not direct the engine to rely on a copy that has not undergone the specified durability step. Manifests serve as the published description of placement in this proposal; no particular manifest layout or publication implementation is stated.
Why not publish the manifest as soon as copying starts?

That would reverse the proposed order. Copy-fsync-then-publish is intended to avoid exposing the new placement before the copied data has been fsynced. The proposal is sensitive to crashes between steps: the engine cannot assume a migration ran to completion before a crash. This ordering alone does not settle every recovery question, but it identifies the durability condition before publication.
If a crash occurs after the copy is fsynced but before publication, what can we conclude from the proposal?

We can conclude only that the proposed order has not yet made the new placement visible through the manifest, even though the copy has passed its fsync step. The engine still needs to preserve acknowledged writes and snapshot-required versions at that transition. The proposal does not specify precisely how recovery treats an unpublished copy, so I would not claim a particular recovery outcome beyond that required preservation.
And if publication has occurred, does the proposal immediately permit removal of the prior copy?

Not merely because of publication. Publishing a migrated placement and reclaiming a version have different conditions. Reclamation is pin-gated: if a snapshot still requires a version, the proposal cannot treat manifest publication alone as permission to discard it. A crash at that boundary must still leave acknowledged writes and snapshot-required versions intact.
How do concurrent writes complicate the copy-and-publish sequence?

The engine cannot assume that a copied set of versions remains unchanged while migration proceeds. The WAL proposal addresses acknowledgment of versioned writes, while manifest publication governs placement, and snapshot pins constrain what reclamation may remove. Their interaction must preserve the correct snapshot view and acknowledged writes despite overlap. The proposal does not yet specify the coordination rule for a write racing with a particular copy or publication step.
Is it fair to describe the manifest as the place where the engine announces a migrated copy, rather than as the thing that makes the write durable?

Yes. In this proposal, copy-fsync-then-publish manifests concern the visibility of a placement change. Fsync-before-ack MVCC WAL concerns the durability ordering for acknowledged writes. Keeping those roles distinct helps avoid treating a newly published location as a substitute for the write-acknowledgment requirement, or treating a durable WAL record as permission to reclaim a version still needed by a snapshot.
Where does read-priority migration throttling come in?

It is the performance-oriented part of the proposal. Migration can compete with reads, so read-priority throttling would give reads priority while limiting migration activity. Its purpose is to help keep migration’s increase in p99 read latency to at most 20% compared with an identical workload without migration. Naming that policy is not evidence that it achieves the limit; the comparison would still need to be established.
Does ‘read-priority’ mean migration must stop whenever a read arrives?

The proposal does not state that specific rule. It says to use read-priority migration throttling, which conveys a preference for reads when controlling migration’s impact, but leaves the precise throttling behavior open. What matters to the stated goal is the resulting p99 read latency under migration relative to the identical no-migration workload.
Could we use throttling to trade away the crash-safety requirements for better p99 latency?

No. Throttling concerns how migration competes with reads; it does not relax durability or reclamation safety. At every migration and reclamation transition, acknowledged writes and snapshot-required versions must survive crashes. The 20% p99 bound is an additional requirement, not an alternative to that one.
Which parts of this proposal speak directly to reclamation, rather than migration?

Durable snapshot pins and pin-gated reclamation speak most directly to whether an older version may be discarded. The copy-fsync-then-publish order speaks directly to making a migrated placement visible, and the WAL speaks to acknowledged writes. They intersect: migration must not create a gap in availability, and reclamation must not erase a snapshot-required version simply because migration has changed where copies reside.
So this is a division of responsibilities, not five independent guarantees?

Right. Each element addresses a different part of the problem, but the required outcome depends on their interaction. For example, an acknowledged write may overlap migration, while a snapshot still needs an older version and reclamation is being considered. WAL durability, published placement, and durable reclamation protection must be consistent through that overlap and through a crash. The proposal identifies the mechanisms to use; it does not claim those interactions have already been proved correct.
What should we avoid claiming just from this list of mechanisms?

We should not claim that every crash transition has been covered by a specified recovery protocol, that concurrent races have been resolved in implementation detail, or that read-priority throttling has measured p99 overhead within 20%. Those are the outcomes the tiered MVCC design must support, but the proposal gives the approach rather than completed validation. We can state the intended order and responsibilities precisely without inventing those missing details.
Can you restate the proposal in one connected sentence, keeping the sequencing clear?

Use an MVCC WAL fsynced before acknowledging writes, durable snapshot pins to protect versions snapshots still require, migration that copies and fsyncs before publishing placement through manifests, reclamation gated by those pins, and read-priority migration throttling aimed at the p99 read-latency limit. The combination is intended to preserve snapshot isolation and crash survival during concurrent migration, writes, and reclamation while limiting migration’s read-tail impact; whether it satisfies every requirement remains to be established.
Which durable ordering keeps concurrently written, snapshot-pinned versions reachable across manifest publication and extent reclamation?

That is the key ordering question left by the proposed mechanisms. Fsync-before-ack covers acknowledged MVCC writes, durable pins record continuing snapshot needs, and copy-fsync-then-publish orders a migrated copy before its manifest publication. But we still need to establish how those durable events relate to one another when a write overlaps publication and an old extent is about to be reclaimed. At every crash point, recovery must be able to reach each acknowledged write and each snapshot-required version; having its bytes somewhere durable is not enough if the durable placement information no longer leads to it.
Can we say the copied extent is safe to rely on once it has been fsynced?

The fsync addresses durability of the copy, but not by itself whether that copy is reachable through the published manifest after a crash. The proposed sequence places copying and fsync before publication. The question is how to ensure that the publication and any subsequent reclamation leave a durable route to every required version, including one written concurrently.
What distinction are you making between a durable version and a reachable version?

A durable version has survived the relevant persistence step; a reachable version is one the engine can still identify and use for the appropriate snapshot after recovery. An extent could retain bytes while a recovered view of placement fails to identify them. Conversely, placement information could point to data that had not yet been made durable. The ordering needs to rule out both kinds of gap for acknowledged writes and snapshot-pinned versions.
Where do the durable snapshot pins enter that ordering?

They must continue to express a snapshot’s need when reclamation is considered, including after a crash. A pin-gated decision cannot safely depend only on a need that disappears from the durable state during a transition. The open question is how the durable pin, the manifest state, and the state used to decide whether an extent can be reclaimed remain consistent with one another.
Is ‘do not reclaim a pinned version’ enough as the complete answer?

It states an essential restriction, but it leaves out reachability. A pinned version must not merely avoid deletion; a snapshot must still be able to find it across manifest publication and recovery. The same ordering also has to account for a concurrent write that may not be represented by the copy made earlier in migration. Those interactions are what the question is asking us to resolve.
Suppose a write happens while an extent is being copied. What must the ordering account for without assuming a particular implementation?

It must account for the possibility that the copy and the concurrent write represent different moments. If that write is acknowledged, the fsync-before-ack MVCC WAL proposal supplies its stated durability ordering, but the overall design must still make the acknowledged version reachable after publication and a crash. We cannot infer from ‘copy-fsync-then-publish’ alone exactly how that version is associated with the published placement.
Could the manifest be published and then the old extent reclaimed simply because the new copy was fsynced first?

Not on that fact alone. Before extent reclamation, the design would need to establish that no snapshot-required version loses its reachable location and that concurrent acknowledged writes remain recoverable. The fsynced copy and published manifest are relevant, but neither fact alone settles whether the old extent still contains a version that must be retained or remains part of its recovery path.
So are there two ordering boundaries to examine: publication and reclamation?

Yes. Across publication, ask whether recovery can identify the required versions despite a concurrent write or an interrupted migration. Across reclamation, ask whether removing the old extent could eliminate the last reachable durable location of any acknowledged or snapshot-required version. A crash immediately on either side of each boundary must preserve the required versions.
Does the pin tell us where the pinned version is?

Not necessarily from what has been stated. The proposal calls for durable snapshot pins, but does not specify their representation or whether a pin itself identifies a location. It is safer to separate the pin’s role—expressing that the snapshot still requires the version—from the manifest’s role in publishing placement. The question is how the durable states work together so the requirement can be honored.
What would a useful crash-point question sound like at the moment a manifest becomes published?

‘If the engine crashes at this publication transition, can recovery still find every acknowledged write and every version required by a durable snapshot pin?’ That question has to include a write concurrent with migration, not just versions present when copying began. It also avoids assuming that successful publication alone establishes the answer.
And at the point an extent is reclaimed?

Ask whether a crash at that transition could leave a required version with neither a retained extent nor another durable, reachable path. Also ask whether the durable snapshot-pin state still prevents removal of versions snapshots need. The extent should not be treated as disposable solely because a manifest change was published; reclaimability is a separate issue.
Can we state the exact durable sequence now?

Not completely from the stated proposal. It names fsync-before-ack WAL, durable pins, copy-fsync-then-publish manifests, and pin-gated reclamation, but it does not specify the full coordination between a concurrent write, publication, and the decision to reclaim an extent. We can state the required property of any sequence: after a crash at every transition, acknowledged writes and snapshot-required versions must remain durable and reachable. Choosing an exact ordering that establishes that property is the unresolved question.
Would it be misleading to answer only ‘copy, fsync, publish, reclaim’?

Yes. That shorthand omits the WAL’s ordering relative to acknowledgment, the durable pins’ protection of snapshot-required versions, and the effect of writes concurrent with copying or publication. It also makes reclamation sound automatic after publication, whereas the proposal calls for pin-gated reclamation and the goal requires crash survival at that transition.
Does this ordering question concern the read-latency limit as well?

Its immediate focus is durability and reachability across publication and extent reclamation. The tiered engine also has the separate requirement that migration raise p99 read latency by at most 20% versus an identical workload without migration, and the proposal includes read-priority migration throttling for that concern. Throttling, however, does not answer which durable ordering protects concurrently written, snapshot-pinned versions.

Let me check my wording: the unresolved issue is not whether to fsync a copy, but whether each transition leaves a crash-recoverable path to all required versions, even as writes and reclamation overlap publication.

That captures it. The copy-fsync-then-publish order is already part of the proposal; the question asks how to integrate it with fsync-before-ack MVCC writes, durable snapshot pins, and pin-gated extent reclamation so that concurrently written, snapshot-pinned versions stay reachable through every relevant crash point. The exact durable ordering that achieves that integration has not been specified here.

I have a hypothesis for the durable ordering: persisted snapshot pins and WAL, followed by copy-fsync, WAL-tail replay, manifest-fsync, then reclamation, should yield zero missing versions under crash injection. Does that address the reachability question?

It proposes an answer to it, but remains a hypothesis rather than an observed result. In the stated order, snapshot pins and the WAL are persisted first; the copied data is then fsynced; the WAL tail is replayed; the manifest is fsynced; and reclamation comes last. The proposed outcome is zero missing versions under crash injection, including versions affected by concurrent writes and snapshot pins. Whether that outcome actually holds at every relevant interruption point still needs to be established.
Why put persisted snapshot pins and the WAL at the front?

They represent two things that must not be lost while placement changes: a snapshot’s continuing need for versions, and the record of MVCC writes. Putting their persistence before the later migration and reclamation steps is meant to keep those obligations present across a crash. That explains the hypothesized ordering; it does not alone prove that every required version remains reachable.
Is ‘persisted snapshot pins and WAL’ a claim that a crash test has already confirmed they work?

No. It describes the first durable condition in the proposed sequence. The claim that this sequence yields zero missing versions under crash injection is still hypothetical. We should not turn the proposed outcome into a reported measurement or say that any crash-injection run has already passed.
What is the copy-fsync step contributing after those are persisted?

It places the migrated copy’s durability step before the manifest’s durability step. That matters because a manifest that points to migrated placement should not be relied on before the copy has undergone its stated fsync. The hypothesis also includes WAL-tail replay before manifest-fsync, so copy-fsync is not being treated as sufficient to account for concurrent writes by itself.
Can you explain the role of WAL-tail replay without assuming how it is implemented?

The tail is the portion relevant to writes that may overlap the copying interval. Replaying it in the proposed sequence is meant to account for writes that the earlier copy might not reflect. The node does not specify a replay algorithm, a cutoff, or additional persistence steps, so those should remain open rather than be supplied as if they were part of this hypothesis.
Why is WAL-tail replay before manifest-fsync important here?

The proposed order makes replay precede the durable publication of the manifest. Its intended logic is that the manifest should not become the durable description of placement while relevant concurrent writes have been left out of the transition. Whether that ordering actually ensures a crash-recoverable path for every such version is precisely what the zero-missing-versions hypothesis puts in question.
And what does manifest-fsync mark in this sequence?

It is the specified durability step for the manifest after copying and WAL-tail replay. That makes the proposed placement information durable before reclamation is attempted. We should not infer a particular manifest format or recovery algorithm from that name; the hypothesis states the ordering and the expected crash-injection outcome, not those implementation details.
Does putting reclamation last mean it is always safe immediately after manifest-fsync?

Not automatically. ‘Then reclamation’ places reclamation after the preceding steps; it does not eliminate the need to respect snapshot pins or to preserve the required versions at that transition. The hypothesis is that the full ordering can yield zero missing versions under crash injection, including around reclamation. That is a property to check, not a conclusion that manifest-fsync alone makes every extent disposable.
What exactly would ‘zero missing versions’ mean in the context of this hypothesis?

It is the proposed crash-injection outcome: after interruption at the relevant transitions, no version that must be retained is missing. In the surrounding design goal, that includes acknowledged writes and versions still required by snapshots. The phrase does not say that every historical version must remain forever, nor does it report a count already observed in an experiment.
Could a version’s data survive a crash yet still count as missing?

Yes, if the version is not reachable for the snapshot or write obligation it must serve. The ordering question is about keeping concurrently written, snapshot-pinned versions reachable across manifest publication and extent reclamation, not merely leaving some bytes on storage. The hypothesis predicts zero missing versions in that meaningful sense, but it does not yet demonstrate it.
If crash injection is mentioned, should we say which exact crash points were tested?

No exact tested crash points are given, and no completed test is reported. We can say that the hypothesis concerns crashes during the ordering—particularly the transitions around copy-fsync, WAL-tail replay, manifest-fsync, and reclamation—but we should not invent an injection schedule or present any outcome as measured.
How should we speak about a crash between WAL-tail replay and manifest-fsync?

As a case the hypothesis needs to withstand, not as a case whose recovery behavior has already been established. The WAL and pins have been persisted earlier in the proposed sequence, while manifest-fsync has not yet occurred. The requirement remains that acknowledged writes and snapshot-required versions be recoverable; the statement of the hypothesis does not provide enough detail to declare exactly how recovery handles that interruption.
What about a crash after manifest-fsync but during reclamation?

That is another critical transition for the proposed zero-missing-versions outcome. The manifest has passed its fsync step, but reclamation must still avoid removing the last reachable durable path to a required version and must respect persisted snapshot pins. The hypothesis says the ordering should yield zero missing versions under crash injection; it does not state that this particular interruption has already been shown safe.
Does WAL-tail replay replace fsync-before-ack for concurrent writes?

No. The earlier proposal calls for an MVCC WAL fsynced before acknowledging a write. WAL-tail replay is a later step in this hypothesized migration ordering, aimed at accounting for writes that overlap copying. They have different roles: replay should not be read as permission to acknowledge a write before its required WAL persistence.
Would the hypothesis establish the p99 read-latency requirement if it proved true?

No. Zero missing versions under crash injection is a crash-safety and reachability outcome. The separate goal is that migration increase p99 read latency by at most 20% versus an identical workload without migration. This ordering hypothesis does not report or predict a p99 measurement, and a successful crash-injection result would not by itself establish that latency bound.
I want a concise statement that keeps the sequence and uncertainty intact.

Hypothesis: persist snapshot pins and the MVCC WAL, then fsync the migrated copy, replay the WAL tail, fsync the manifest, and only then perform reclamation; this ordering is expected to yield zero missing versions under crash injection. It is a proposed crash-safety outcome, not a completed test result.
What should we do next to work out the durable ordering across migration and reclamation?

The plan is to specify durable migration invariants first, implement WAL-tail replay and pin-gated reclamation, and then crash-test every fsync boundary while writes and snapshots are concurrent. That order matters: the invariants state what must remain true, the implementation supplies the proposed behavior, and the crash tests examine interruptions at the durability boundaries.
What do you mean by a durable migration invariant?

It is a condition that must still hold after a crash interrupts migration. For this engine, the central concern is that acknowledged writes and versions required by snapshots remain recoverable and reachable as placement changes and extents become candidates for reclamation. Stating that condition explicitly gives the implementation and crash tests something precise to address; it does not assume they already satisfy it.
Why specify the invariants before implementing the replay and reclamation pieces?

Otherwise, it would be easy to describe the mechanics without being clear about the required outcome at each durable transition. The invariants should make clear what cannot be lost, even when a write overlaps migration or a snapshot still needs an older version. WAL-tail replay and pin-gated reclamation can then be considered against those conditions rather than treated as sufficient merely because they have been implemented.
Should the invariants talk only about whether the data survives?

They should also address reachability. A version could remain on storage yet be unavailable to recovery or to the snapshot that needs it. The migration invariants need to cover the durable path by which acknowledged and snapshot-required versions can still be found across manifest publication and extent reclamation.
Is it enough to state one invariant for the final state of migration?

No. The plan calls for durable migration invariants, and the concern is crashes during transitions, not just after migration is complete. They need to be meaningful at the fsync boundaries that will later be crash-tested. A final state that looks correct would not, on its own, show that an interrupted transition is safe.
Where does WAL-tail replay fit in the implementation part of the plan?

It is one of the two implementation tasks named here. Its role is to account for writes concurrent with migration that an earlier copy might not reflect. The plan is to implement it, then examine its behavior under crashes at the fsync boundaries while writes and snapshots overlap. This node does not specify its algorithm or claim that it has already been implemented.
And what exactly is planned for reclamation?

Implement pin-gated reclamation. The gate is intended to prevent reclaiming a version while a snapshot still requires it. Its durable behavior matters because a crash during reclamation must not leave a snapshot-required version missing or unreachable. The plan names that implementation work without prescribing a particular pin representation or reclamation algorithm.
Do replay and reclamation have to be considered together?

Yes, when checking the invariants. Replay concerns concurrently written versions that migration must account for; reclamation concerns versions that must not be removed while needed. Manifest publication sits between changing placement and considering old extents for removal. Even if each piece appears sensible in isolation, their interaction across crash points is the reason to specify invariants and run the planned tests.
What does ‘crash-test every fsync boundary’ require us to focus on?

It calls for examining crashes at each fsync boundary in the migration and reclamation path, rather than testing only a completed move or a single convenient interruption. At each boundary, the question is whether recovery can still reach acknowledged writes and snapshot-required versions. The plan does not provide a test harness or report results; it sets the intended scope of crash testing.
Why explicitly require concurrent writes during those crash tests?

Because WAL-tail replay is meant to address writes that overlap migration. Testing only when writes are paused would not exercise that interaction. The plan therefore calls for crash testing at every fsync boundary during concurrent writes, so the required durability of acknowledged versions is examined under the overlap that motivates replay.
Why include concurrent snapshots as well?

Snapshots create the requirement to retain particular MVCC versions even as migration and reclamation proceed. Including concurrent snapshots exercises the pin-gated reclamation condition and the requirement that snapshot-needed versions remain reachable after a crash. A test without snapshots would not address that part of the plan.
Are these tests meant to establish that fsync alone makes reclamation safe?

No. An fsync boundary is a place to test interruption, not a blanket permission to reclaim. The invariants still have to hold, and reclamation remains pin-gated. The tests should examine whether the implemented behavior preserves required versions across those boundaries; the plan does not presume a passing result.
Could we skip the invariant specification and just look for missing versions after crash tests?

That would leave the intended guarantee less clear. The plan explicitly starts by specifying durable migration invariants, then implements the named mechanisms, then crash-tests. Defining what must remain durable and reachable helps interpret a test outcome, especially when a version is old but still required by a snapshot or when a write was acknowledged during migration.
Does this plan itself choose an exact answer to the durable-ordering question?

It is a way to resolve that question, not a declaration that it has already been resolved. The invariants will state the required properties, WAL-tail replay and pin-gated reclamation are to be implemented, and crash testing at every fsync boundary during concurrent writes and snapshots will probe the result. The node does not give a completed proof, implementation, or crash-test outcome.

Not as though it were included in this particular plan.
